topics.title: [Brainstorm] Project Matchmaker — An Agent-Assisted Collaboration Network for the CKB Ecosystem

recent_posts.topic_title: [Brainstorm] Project Matchmaker — An Agent-Assisted Collaboration Network for the CKB Ecosystem
recent_posts.author: ArthurZhang
recent_posts.content_text:
During a brainstorming session with Matt, Shawn, Leigh, Yukun and a few others, I brought up an idea that I think could be worth exploring.
We have quite a few promising projects and talented developers across the CKB ecosystem, but many of them are working in relative isolation. Sometimes two teams are solving closely related problems without knowing it. Other times, a project needs precisely the expertise that somebody elsewhere in the community already has.
What if we built a platform that continuously looks for these connections?
Let’s call it Project Matchmaker for now. This is just a brainstorming proposal, not an agreed roadmap.
The product
Imagine a shared directory of developers, projects, repositories and ongoing research, with a few AI agents working behind the scenes.
Developers could register their skills, interests, availability and preferred areas of contribution. Projects could describe what they’re building, their dependencies, outstanding problems and where they need help.
The agents would then analyse potential synergies across the ecosystem and produce a daily or weekly collaboration report.
For example:
Project A has developed a reusable ZK verification component that Project B could integrate.
Project C needs someone familiar with CKB transaction composition, while Developer D has recently been working on precisely that.
Two teams are implementing similar infrastructure and might benefit from sharing a library rather than maintaining separate implementations.
A newly announced project has architectural dependencies or research interests that overlap with three existing teams.
When a new project makes its debut, the platform could automatically generate a short collaboration opportunity report, suggesting relevant developers, existing projects, reusable components and potential contributors.
Possible architecture
I imagine a relatively straightforward system built around a continuously updated knowledge graph.
1. Discovery layer: Collect information from public GitHub repositories, issues, Nervos Talk discussions and voluntarily submitted developer/project profiles. Private community data would require explicit permission.
2. Knowledge graph: Represent developers, projects, skills, protocol components, dependencies and open problems as connected entities, with links back to supporting evidence.
3. Agent layer: Run specialised agents for project discovery, technical capability analysis, collaboration matching and opportunity reporting. Matching could combine semantic search with graph relationships, rather than relying entirely on an LLM’s judgement.
4. Product layer: A searchable community directory, project onboarding, personalised collaboration suggestions and a regular ecosystem synergy digest.
Importantly, every recommendation should explain why two parties might benefit from working together, with links to actual code, issues or research. People should be able to correct recommendations, decline introductions and control their own availability.
this is purely a brainstorm. I’d love to hear whether people think this would actually be useful, what existing tools we could build upon, and whether anyone would be interested in experimenting with a prototype.

recent_posts.author: SalmanDev
recent_posts.content_text:
Tranfr — Progress Update
The recovery lock contract has now been deployed to CKB testnet, and the build and deployment steps are documented so anyone can reproduce the deployment independently.
Completed so far
Deployed the recovery lock contract to CKB testnet.
Documented the build and deployment process for reproducibility.
Built most of the TypeScript developer toolkit on top of the contract, including:
Recovery eligibility checks.
Lock status and time-remaining queries.
Creation of new protected locks.
Lock renewal and recovery-recipient updates.
Added automated tests covering these implemented operations.
This establishes the deployed contract and most of the developer-facing functionality needed to integrate Tranfr into applications.
Next steps
The remaining implementation work is focused on completing the two final contract actions:
Owner reclaim: Allow the owner to take back the locked funds.
Recipient claim: Allow the designated recovery recipient to claim the funds after the deadline.
Once these are implemented, I’ll focus on end-to-end validation and delivery:
Test the complete recovery lifecycle on CKB testnet.
Build a demo web page demonstrating the full flow.
Complete the security write-up, technical documentation, and integration guidance.
The goal is to deliver a reproducible, testnet-deployed recovery primitive with a developer toolkit, a working end-to-end demonstration, and sufficient documentation for independent testing and integration.

topics.title: Spark Program | NNCBN - Nervos Network Community Boot Nodes

recent_posts.topic_title: Spark Program | NNCBN - Nervos Network Community Boot Nodes
recent_posts.author: NNCBN
recent_posts.content_text:
2026 October 13, Third Weekly Report
The device has now arrived and is already running Qubes OS. The CPU usage in idle mode is less than 1%! This device is already an integral part of my journey, and I very much hope it will continue to operate in 2027 and well into the future to support the Nervos Network.
Decision against the blanket recommendation of unpartitioned storage space for overprovisioning.
SSD manufacturers¹ distinguish between read-intensive and write-intensive applications when it comes to over-provisioning. The initial synchronization of the blockchain places a particularly heavy load on the SSD, but this lasts only until the node is fully synchronized. During subsequent normal operation, access is primarily to various storage areas, with write operations occurring continuously but to a lesser extent.
If you use an SSD with a high write load, you can leave a portion of its capacity—for example, about 10%—unpartitioned as a precaution, so that the controller has additional headroom for internal storage management. This is a practical precaution, not an official requirement:
The actual benefit depends on the SSD model, and some drives already have built-in reserve space. Free, unallocated space can give an SSD additional leeway for internal management processes during write operations; however, the benefit depends on the drive, its fill level, and the actual amount of data being written.
We have therefore decided not to burden the user with partitioning recommendations. The current wording in the official documentation is already well-chosen: An SSD is recommended for faster synchronization than traditional hard drives. It must also be large enough to provide sufficient free space. If you want to create additional buffer space, you can leave part of the SSD unpartitioned. However, this is a precautionary measure and not an official recommendation. As an example of a free, unpartitioned area, I’ll choose 10% instead of the 20% I originally had in mind, since the CKB node typically doesn’t experience very high load, and storage manufacturers already include overprovisioned storage that remains invisible to the user.
In my specific case, for the first community boot node, I’ve installed a high-quality, brand-name 1,000-gigabyte SSD from Kingston. The computer I purchased for the boot node is high-quality and comes with brand-name memory. We do not create an unpartitioned overprovisioning area in our Qubes OS boot node installation guide.
nn2026-10-13 13-03-081062×717 123 KB
I wrote the step-by-step installation guide in two languages. Although there is no German-language section on the forum, a large portion of the Nervos network nodes are already located in German-speaking countries, and it requires little extra effort on my part, since I have lived in German-speaking countries and am very fluent in the language.
I wrote and updated the first draft of the step-by-step installation guide in shared cloud documents. For best formatting, view it in the browser’s desktop mode. I’d also be happy to create a thread here in the forum with clear formatting. It’s easier to ask questions and quote text passages here. I’ll create this at a later date, and it will be in English only, possibly with a link to the German text document.
-

topics.title: Spark Program | CKB-VM Sail Validation Sprint：可复现的 RISC-V 语义差分工具、Lean 4 证明与 Rocq/Coq 兼容性 Spike

recent_posts.topic_title: Spark Program | CKB-VM Sail Validation Sprint：可复现的 RISC-V 语义差分工具、Lean 4 证明与 Rocq/Coq 兼容性 Spike
recent_posts.author: TinyuengKwan
recent_posts.content_text:
跟社区同步一下 CKB-VM Sail Validation Sprint 的交付进展。week6-0.2.0 已经发布，代码、证据和复现说明都在公开仓库。先说清楚范围：这是重新申请时约定的六周 MVP，不是整个 CKB-VM 的正确性证明。
1. 差分工具：33 个案例逐步一致
在固定的 CKB-VM VERSION2 Rust 解释器和 Sail RISC-V 模型之间，对同一条注入指令流逐步比较提交效果。ADD 13、ADDI 10、BEQ 10，共 33 个案例、398 步全部一致，每个案例都能单独重放。比较器本身也测过：往轨迹里注入 6 类错误共 194 次，全部被检出并定位到字段。
对维护者来说，它能告诉你两边从哪一步、哪个字段开始分歧，并保留可重放的输入；但它不保证语料之外没有缺陷。
想自己跑一下（需要已装好 Rust、OPAM 和常规构建依赖；第一次要从源码构建 Sail，耗时看机器和网络）：
git clone --recursive https://github.com/TinyuengKwan/ckb-vm-sail-verify && cd ckb-vm-sail-verify
git checkout week6-0.2.0 && git submodule update --init --recursive
make ckb-baseline-apply
make sail-compiler && export PATH="$HOME/.local/share/sail-src/bin:$PATH"
make verify-env && make verify-dii
cargo run -p ckb-vm-sail-diff -- --replay artifacts/corpus/add-signed-overflow.json
2. 条件性 ADD 证明（Lean 4）
Lean 4 定理直接连接生产 Rust 入口和 Sail 生成的定义，覆盖 ADD 的寄存器效果、x0 写入抑制和 PC 更新；另一条定理从同一个 32 位原始编码出发，证明两侧解码出相同的 ADD。两条都由 kernel 检查，不依赖 sorryAx，但带着明确记录的外部声明和状态前提，所以是条件性证明。取指、物理内存对应、平台启动可达性、cycle、MOP、ASM/JIT 都不在结论内；ADDI、BEQ 目前只有运行时证据。细节见覆盖矩阵和证明前提。
还有两点要提前说：验证对象是上游 commit 加一份受审的容器化补丁（把三个动态字段收进私有结构，方便提取），不是原样的上游代码；Rocq/Coq 路线的结论是可复现的 NO-GO，附最小复现，不计入证明。
3. 可恢复的发布
0.2.0 在全新 Ubuntu 24.04 KVM guest 里从零跑完 11 个阶段（重新生成、测试、差分、完整 Lean 门禁、Rocq spike），约 2.5 小时，全部通过；CI 接收并校验了证据包、重放了案例。发布包含主包、签名和固定工具包，tag 已签名，release 不可变，按说明可以离线恢复出同一套源码和工具（工具要求固定安装路径）。
需要区分的是：VM 运行是项目侧做的，CI 只做了接收和重放，都不算第三方复现。按当前仓库的发布政策，项目侧发布验收已通过，第三方复现记为 deferred；这不代表独立复现已完成，也不代替 Spark 委员会的最终判断。（0.1.0 是 9 月 30 日按旧流程发布的同一份代码，原样保留。）
4. 欢迎独立复现
希望 CKB 官方或其指定、独立于项目维护者的人员，在自己的全新环境里按复现说明跑一遍，交回日志和签名声明。流程以 main 上更新后的说明为准，运行对象仍是发布候选本身。复现失败也请保留首次失败日志，我会协助定位，但不会靠换候选或放宽检查来保住结论。
最想听到维护者意见的三件事：补丁能否接受、ADD 定理的前提是否清晰合理、发布包能否在你们的环境里重现。后续扩大覆盖再单独讨论。

recent_posts.topic_title: Noir-CKB update: what I decided after the direction check, what you can try today, and where this is going
recent_posts.author: xiaomao
recent_posts.content_text:
About a month ago I shared a direction check here for noir-ckb, asking for feedback on what I was building. I got really thoughtful replies, mostly around two questions:
Where should a proof live in a CKB transaction (Lock or Type?), and is Noir → Groth16 even the right backend, given its per-circuit trusted setup.
This post is the follow-up: what I decided, what exists now that you can actually run (including on testnet), and the longer-term picture of where I want this to go. It’s a long one, sorry in advance
Quick recap, if you’re new to this
noir-ckb lets you write a rule in Noir, prove it off-chain, and have a CKB script verify the proof. The sentence that has driven the whole project is:
> A proof that verifies is not the same as a proof that authorizes this Cell transition.
A Groth16 proof can be mathematically perfect and still be about the wrong thing: the wrong Cell, the wrong state change, the wrong network. So the interesting work isn’t only verifying proofs on CKB-VM, it’s binding each proof to the exact transaction it’s attached to, so that a valid proof can’t be reused anywhere else.
Decision 1: where the proof lives
In my reply in that thread I ended up with four possible patterns:
Proof-only Lock for a stateless cell: having a valid proof is the permission to spend.
Generic verifier Lock + binding Type: the Lock checks the proof, the Type checks the proof is about this exact transition. (My earlier Capsule prototype.)
Normal ownership Lock + proof-verifying Type: a signature decides who can spend; the Type verifies the proof and binds it to the state change.
Two proofs, one in the Lock and one in the Type, tied together by shared context.
Where they ended up:
Pattern 3 is now live on testnet, as a small owned counter. A normal secp256k1 Lock controls who may spend the Cell. The counter’s Type Script rebuilds the expected public statement from the actual transaction (network, the consumed Cell, old and new value, successor Lock and capacity) and only then verifies the Groth16 proof. A perfectly valid proof for a different Cell, a different change or a different network gets rejected. The local test suite throws 48 of those attacks at it in CKB-VM, plus three deliberately broken contracts that the tests have to catch.
I’ll be honest about the counter, though: its proof is redundant. Every input is public, so the Type could just check `new = old + 1` itself in a few instructions instead of about 111 million cycles. It proves the plumbing and the binding work. It doesn’t show why you’d want zero knowledge.
So the next example is a stateful version of pattern 1:
A private tally. The Cell holds a commitment to a hidden 64-bit number. Whoever knows a secret key can add a hidden amount (including zero, so an update doesn’t even reveal whether anything was added). There’s no signature: the proof is the permission, and the logic lives in a Type so the state survives each update.
That’s where binding stops being a nice-to-have and becomes the entire security model. With no signature, a proof copied out of the mempool is the only thing between an attacker and your tally, so it has to commit to one consumed Cell, one old and new commitment, one successor and one network. Then it’s useless anywhere else.
What it won’t hide, to be upfront: updates to one Cell are still linkable to each other, and the number of updates, their timing and who paid the fee are public. Fully unlinkable updates would need a shielded pool, which is a different design.
The design is written and accepted, not built yet. Before committing to it I checked the risky parts against the current backend: the hash library that works with my compiler version has a known bug for longer inputs, so every hash in the design takes three inputs or fewer, and a differential test (Noir’s own execution vs. the backend’s constraint system) agreed on all 19 cases I threw at it.
Patterns 2 and 4 are parked for now. I’d rather build them when a real application needs them.
Decision 2: staying with Noir → Groth16 (for now)
It was suggested that I look at the optimized SP1 verifier for CKB-VM, because SP1’s PLONK setup is universal, so no per-circuit ceremony. I took that seriously: I reproduced its verification on CKB-VM (about 66M cycles for the upstream fixture) and a set of rejection cases. It works.
The problem is one step earlier. SP1 proves programs compiled for its zkVM; it doesn’t take Noir circuits. Keeping Noir would mean building a Noir-to-SP1 bridge first (for example, running an ACIR interpreter inside SP1), which I couldn’t find and which would be a whole project on its own. Rewriting circuits in Rust would mean dropping the Noir workflow this project exists for.
So I’m staying with Noir → Groth16 and paying the setup cost properly, with a ceremony (more below). That’s a scoping decision, not a verdict that SP1 is worse. If a Noir path to SP1 appears, the binding layer is the part I’d expect to carry over.
What you can try today
Everything is in one guide: noir-ckb-verifier/docs/try-the-counter.md at main · wamimi/noir-ckb-verifier · GitHub
Part 1, locally, no wallet, no money. One command compiles the circuit, generates a fresh proof, starts a throwaway CKB chain on your computer, and sends real signed transactions that deploy the contract, create a counter and update it with the proof. It runs on Apple Silicon Macs and Ubuntu 24.04 (x86_64 and ARM64), natively or in a container. (Intel Macs and Windows aren’t supported yet.)
Part 2, your own counter on testnet. You don’t deploy anything: the contract and verification key are already on testnet and the proving files are published, so it costs about 262 testnet CKB from the faucet (200 stay locked in your counter, because this demo contract has no withdraw). Before you sign anything, the tool checks that the published files are exactly what’s deployed, that the code on testnet matches them byte for byte, and that your own machine compiles the circuit to the same thing. Then you review, sign and send each transaction yourself with your own `ckb-cli` account. The proof is generated on your machine.
I went through it from a brand new account:
- created at 0: [0x0b6efcd7…888798c](https://testnet.explorer.nervos.org/transaction/0x0b6efcd70f111afd1c885557c84f7b93ef4ee8401dd9fe258b9fb677c888798c)
- updated 0 → 1 with a proof made on my laptop: [0xe6589170…0089126f](https://testnet.explorer.nervos.org/transaction/0xe6589170381a02a249c37be8ab279e6229e2feb8f177f3d572bc63f30089126f)
Doing it as a “stranger” found a couple of rough edges that I fixed straight away. I’m sure you’ll find more, and I’d love to hear about them.
The trust part, plainly
The counter’s keys came from a single-party development setup, made by me. In principle that means I could forge counter proofs. For the counter it’s tolerable, because every update also needs your signature, so nobody can change your counter without your key.
For the private tally it’s not tolerable, since the proof is the only authority. So before the tally goes to testnet I’ll run a small public setup ceremony. It’s a relay where each person downloads the latest file, runs one `snarkjs` command on their laptop (around ten minutes), and posts the hash it prints. If even one contributor throws away their randomness, nobody can forge proofs. A future CKB block hash gets mixed in at the end so nobody can steer the result, and anyone can verify the whole transcript afterwards.
I’m looking for around five contributors(or more) If you’d like to be one, reply here or DM me and I’ll send instructions once the circuit is frozen. (It’s for a testnet developer preview, not an audited production ceremony.)
## Where I want this to go
This is the part I’m most excited about. The developer experience I’m working toward:
> You start a project, bring a supported Noir circuit, declare how its public values map to your Cells, and the tool builds the artifacts, the Type Script and an adversarial test suite for you. You test it locally, deploy to testnet, and connect it to your frontend, where your users generate proofs in their own browser and authorize updates with their own wallet.
Almost none of that exists yet beyond the counter, so here is how I’m thinking about getting there, step by step:
1. A real developer toolkit, natively. Turn today’s reference workflow into an installable CLI that works outside this repository, with clear diagnostics and an explicit list of what’s supported. Then support a project within one well-defined pattern (one owner-controlled Cell transitioning to one successor): a config file for how your public values map to Cell state, early and clear errors when a circuit uses something the backend doesn’t support, and artifact manifests so you can always tell which circuit, key, contract and toolchain belong together. A second small example should build from its own folder without touching toolkit code; that’s the real test of reuse.
2. Proving in the browser, with a wallet. This is where it gets fun, and also where I want to be careful. NoirJS can execute a circuit in the browser and produce a witness, but my route also needs the witness converted to the backend’s layout and a Groth16 proof from snarkjs. Barretenberg’s browser prover (UltraHonk) is a different proof system, so it can’t just be plugged into the existing CKB verifier. So the first milestone is narrow: a proof generated in a browser for the fixed counter must pass the existing on-chain verifier, and altered statements must still be rejected. Phone performance has to be measured as well. If that works, the acceptance app is a little visitor-owned counter: connect a wallet, create your counter, click increment, prove in the browser, sign, see it confirmed.
3. Applications that push the toolkit. Battleship is the one I keep coming back to (and it’s why pattern 3 matters: the player’s Lock authorizes the move, the Type proves the hit/miss answer is consistent with the committed board). But a proof of one move doesn’t make a fair game by itself: turns, timeouts, repeated shots and endings all need their own design. So it’ll be its own project once the architecture holds up.
4. Grow from real demand. More circuit operations, structured inputs, other wallet locks, multi-Cell patterns: added when an actual application needs them, each with its own compatibility statement and attack tests. Production readiness (a real setup strategy, independent review, upgrade policy) is a separate undertaking from a testnet release, and I won’t blur the two.
## What would help most
Try it and tell me where you got stuck and on which OS: Sign in to GitHub · GitHub (never share wallet folders or passwords, just the error and the manifest file).
If you’re building on CKB: what would you want to prove inside a transaction? Which public values would have to match your Cells? Which of the four patterns fits?
Ceremony: reply if you’d like to contribute.
Browser proving: if you’ve tried NoirJS, snarkjs or wallet signing in a CKB frontend, I’d really like to hear what hurt.
Honestly, this has become one of my favourite things to work on. Each week I understand CKB a little better, and every time something breaks on someone else’s machine, the project gets more real. Thank you to everyone who replied to the direction check: it changed what I built. I’m excited to see where this goes, and I’d love for some of you to come along

topics.title: Tactus O1: First Based EVM Rollup on CKB

recent_posts.topic_title: Tactus O1: First Based EVM Rollup on CKB
recent_posts.author: ArthurZhang
recent_posts.content_text:
A follow-up on Tactus O1. The latest experiments exposed two problems I need to address. Generating a ZK proof took roughly 78 minutes on my laptop, while verification on CKB consumed about 3.985 billion cycles, exceeding mainnet’s 3.5 billion limit. The prototype works on a devnet with a higher limit, but is not mainnet-ready. The prover also replays execution history from genesis, so the cost grows as the chain gets longer.
The other concern is settlement lag. CKB can keep accepting EVM transaction batches while their proofs are still pending. That means transaction ordering can move ahead of verified settlement, potentially delaying withdrawals indefinitely if proving cannot keep up. The priority route has a related limitation: it prevents builders from selectively skipping sealed requests while batches continue, but cannot guarantee timely progress when builders or provers stop cooperating.
I’ve been looking at other based rollups such as Taiko and Igra for comparison. Taiko manages outstanding proposals through bounded queues, prover incentives and L1 forced inclusion, although proving delays can still stall progress. Igra takes a different approach, carrying ordinary EVM transactions all through Kaspa L1 without requiring the same ZK settlement pipeline, but with different execution-verification and custody assumptions. For Tactus, I’m investigating incremental proving, cheaper CKB verification and bounded settlement lag. These are still open research questions.
